feed.title: Combined summary - Quantum Landmines and Vulnerable Coin Auctions

entry.title: Combined summary - Quantum Landmines and Vulnerable Coin Auctions
entry.summary: The increasing threat posed by quantum computing has catalyzed a wave of innovative strategies in cryptocurrency development, focusing on post-quantum (PQ) migration and the protection of legacy coins. Central to these discussions is the anticipation of "Q-day," when quantum computers may be capable of compromising classical cryptography. Before this crucial threshold, developers are considering the deployment of quantum-safe output types and the introduction of new consensus rules via soft forks. These rules would require that any attempt to spend legacy outputs must be fully collateralized and meet additional criteria such as time-based restrictions or alternate spend paths, mechanisms reminiscent of vaults or covenants but uniquely enforced through protocol changes. One of the more inventive proposals involves the concept of "Quantum Landmines," which use a commit/reveal scheme bolstered by punitive measures for theft attempts. Owners can secretly embed proofs tied to their legacy keys within trivial quantum-safe outputs, activating strong defensive measures post-Q-day. If an attacker tries to exploit a vulnerable coin, they are forced to wait out a time window before accessing the funds. During this interval, the rightful owner can reveal their proof and claim both the original coins and the attacker's collateral, introducing a significant deterrent for potential attackers and adding uncertainty regarding which coins are genuinely at risk. Further refinements recognize the limitations of landmine approaches, particularly when many legacy private keys are inaccessible. To mitigate this, the "Staked Auction" model allows users to pre-commit quantum-safe coins as bids on vulnerable outputs. After Q-day, if an attacker spends a legacy coin with collateral, an auction among pre-committed bidders determines who claims a portion of the collateral, while the stolen coins are destroyed. Design choices within this framework—such as bid structure, risk allocation, and collateral management—can be customized, ensuring that attackers cannot reliably profit unless they outperform all legitimate stakers. Expanding on these ideas, the "Sats Auction" mechanism, inspired by Neha Narula and the [Dollar Auction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dollar_auction) game, eliminates the need for pre-Q-day commitments. Each legacy coin spend triggers an open auction after the landmine timeout, where participants continuously bid, risking their own assets to avoid being the second-highest bidder. This dynamic can escalate rapidly, potentially causing attackers to lose all their collateral and enabling some recovery for original owners. The system’s flexibility in determining collateral ratios, bid intervals, and the ultimate fate of forfeited collateral invites further economic experimentation, blending cryptographic safeguards with game-theoretic principles. From a best-practices standpoint, the safest course for users aware of quantum risks is to migrate assets from legacy Bitcoin addresses to quantum-resistant wallets prior to the advent of practical quantum attacks. Deliberately leaving coins exposed serves little purpose except as bait, which introduces unnecessary risk and incentivizes malicious behavior. Proactive security measures should take precedence over relying on complex reactive schemes. An intriguing dimension of the landmine approach is its impact on network transparency. By creating uncertainty around which coins are quantum-safe, this strategy undermines arguments for freezing vulnerable coins and turns the indeterminate state of unspent transaction outputs (UTXOs) into a form of defense. This uncertainty means that even high-profile holdings, such as those attributed to Satoshi, can serve as latent deterrents against quantum theft, since their vulnerability is only revealed upon attempted exploitation. The approach challenges conventional wisdom by suggesting that coexistence with quantum attackers may be feasible if robust economic disincentives are in place, thereby reinforcing Bitcoin's core values through carefully calibrated penalty and reward mechanisms. Critical discussion highlights several unresolved challenges and trade-offs. While making it impossible to ascertain the number of quantum-safe coins adds a layer of unpredictability for attackers, it simultaneously obscures vital metrics needed to gauge PQ migration progress, complicating future protocol decisions. Attackers can focus exclusively on outputs created before protective measures were introduced, sidestepping newer defenses. Questions have arisen about the fairness and logic behind certain auction outcomes, the distinction between attackers and honest users, and the enforceability of staking or collateral requirements. Suggestions include allowing exceptions to collateralization for transactions accompanied by verifiable ownership proofs predating Q-day, thus streamlining rescue operations for legitimate holders. The evolving landscape of quantum defense in decentralized finance relies on a hybridization of cryptographic innovation and incentive engineering. No singular solution stands out as universally optimal, and the ongoing dialogue weighs the merits of freezing coins, redistributing value, or adopting randomized outcomes akin to lotteries. As time passes beyond Q-day, the likelihood increases that spenders of vulnerable outputs are attackers, necessitating adaptive, nuanced protocols. For those seeking deeper engagement, resources such as the [Bitcoin Development Mailing List](https://groups.google.com/forum/!forum/bitcoin-dev) offer continued exploration of these themes. In summary, by leveraging strategic uncertainty, economic deterrence, and flexible consensus mechanisms, the cryptocurrency community is devising sophisticated tools to address the looming quantum threat.
